outcome: Marc Cabanes and Britta Späth proved the McKay conjecture in full generality, for every prime and every finite group, completing the reduction of Isaacs–Malle–Navarro (2007) to a statement about representations of finite simple groups via the classification of finite simple groups; the result was announced in October 2023, posted to arXiv in October 2024, and accepted by the Annals of Mathematics in April 2025 (published 2026).
summary: The McKay conjecture — that for any prime ℓ, the number of irreducible complex characters of a finite group G with degree prime to ℓ equals the same count for the normalizer of a Sylow ℓ-subgroup — has been fully proved by Marc Cabanes and Britta Späth for all primes and all finite groups. I read the arXiv abstract page for 2410.20392 (submitted 2024-10-27, revised 2025-05-01), which states the theorem exactly as above and confirms this closes the reduction that Isaacs, Malle and Navarro established in 2007 (itself building on Späth and Malle's 2016 proof for the prime 2, which predates the frozen revision and was already reflected there). I also read the Annals of Mathematics publication page, which records the paper as received 2024-07-31, revised 2025-04-13, accepted 2025-04-17, and slated for Volume 203, Issue 3 (2026), pp. 933–1032 — journal acceptance by a top journal of record, satisfying the bar for `resolved` rather than `claimed`. I read the Quanta Magazine article (2025-02-19), a clear expert digestion: it recounts the 20-year history of the problem, the announcement to over 100 mathematicians at conferences in October 2023, and describes the proof method (four families of Lie-type groups handled via the classification of finite simple groups) in a way that establishes independent expert confirmation of the result, not just a press release. None of these three primary/secondary sources mentions any AI or machine-learning system in any capacity — not for generating arguments, not for verification, not for formalisation, not even for peripheral tasks like proofreading. The proof is a purely human, classical mathematical achievement built on decades of case-by-case work in the representation theory of finite groups of Lie type. I dated the event to the arXiv posting (2024-10-27) as the first fully public written argument, rather than the October 2023 conference announcements (which were oral/informal and not a written manuscript) or the Annals 'received' date of 2024-07-31 (which reflects private journal submission, not public posting) — all three postdate the frozen revision's cutoff of 2024-01-26 regardless of which is used, so the choice does not affect window classification, only precision. I checked the current Wikipedia article on the McKay conjecture, which now reflects the 2023 announcement and 2024 manuscript. I found no dispute over priority or correctness; Cabanes and Späth are the sole credited authors throughout.
competing_reading: One could argue the event date should be dated to the October 2023 announcement at conferences, since that is when the mathematical community first learned the result existed and when Quanta's account treats the substantive achievement as complete; however, no written argument was public until the 2024 arXiv posting, so I used that per §6.3's instruction to date the first public written argument. Either dating falls after 26 January 2024, so it does not change the status or the fact that this is a genuine post-cutoff resolution.
what_would_settle_it: Nothing further is needed on the mathematical or AI-involvement question; both are settled by the primary sources read. The only open item would be locating the final published Annals PDF (not freely accessible) to double check there is no late-added acknowledgement of computational or AI tools, but the arXiv preprint (the operative public version) shows none, and no secondary source discloses any.
